justification_text:
The point estimates presented in the forecast for 1 day, 1 week, and 1 month ahead are based on the assumption that the underlying trend will persist without significant disruptions. For simplicity, the point estimate remains constant across the three horizons at 221.81. This assumes the central tendency of the forecast is anchored in either recent data patterns (e.g., mean or median) or a stable baseline that reflects the absence of major external shocks. Essentially, this reflects the expectation that, on average, the variable being forecasted will remain close to its current observed value across all timeframes.

The widening of the confidence intervals (90% CI) over time reflects the increasing uncertainty as you look further into the future. Over shorter horizons, variability due to minor fluctuations in observable factors—such as noise in short-term trends or mild day-to-day randomness—results in tighter intervals, evident in the narrower 1-day 90% CI (219.59–224.03). As the time horizon extends to 1 week and especially to 1 month, compounding uncertainties, such as accumulating random noise, longer-term trend shifts, or emerging dynamics, broaden the forecast intervals. Longer-term outcomes are harder to pin down because of the increasing potential influence of unanticipated changes or new variables coming into play.

Despite confidence intervals aiming for 90% coverage, there is always a possibility that certain risks or events could push the actual values outside these intervals. For example, unexpected news or shocks specific to the domain of the forecast (e.g., a macroeconomic event, regulatory change, market disruption, or an unforeseen crisis) could cause significant deviations from the predicted range. These factors introduce "tail risks," which, although less likely, would result in outcomes far outside the anticipated range. Such risks are inherently difficult to model and are not fully captured in the probabilistic framework of this forecast. This is why forecasts should always be supplemented with a recognition of potential outliers and black swan events.
